title: YOU WANT GOD TO BLESS YOUR PLANS… BUT WHAT IF HE NEVER ASKED YOU TO MAKE THEM?
paragraphs: YOU WANT GOD TO BLESS YOUR PLANS… BUT WHAT IF HE NEVER ASKED YOU TO MAKE THEM?

The most frightening thing isn't having a dream that fails. It's achieving everything you prayed for, only to discover that somewhere along the way, you stopped asking whether Jesus was the One you were following.
You prayed about it.
You worked for it.
You lost sleep over it.
You even told people, “I believe God is going to bless this.”
But there is a question that can shake a person's soul when they finally have the courage to ask it.
What if the thing you're asking God to bless is the very thing He's calling you to surrender?
Not because every dream is sinful.
Not because ambition is evil.
Not because God delights in disappointing His children.
But because it is possible to build something impressive while quietly neglecting the One you claim to be building it for.
And perhaps the most dangerous place a Christian can find himself is not in obvious rebellion against God.
It is in a life so busy pursuing good things that he no longer notices how far his heart has drifted from Christ.
Read that again.
Because this may not be about somebody else.
This may be about you.
You have a plan for your career. A plan for your finances. A plan for your family. A plan for your future.
You know where you want to be in five years. You know what you want to accomplish. You know what kind of life you hope to create.
And when you pray, you bring those plans before God.
“Lord, open the door.”
“Lord, make a way.”
“Lord, bless my business.”
“Lord, give me this opportunity.”
“Lord, let this relationship work.”
“Lord, make me successful.”
There is nothing inherently wrong with bringing these desires to your heavenly Father. Scripture actually invites us to bring our concerns to Him.
But somewhere between asking God for help and waiting for His answer, something can happen.
We stop seeking His will.
And start seeking His approval for decisions we have already made.
We don't always say it out loud.
But our prayers begin to sound less like, “Father, what do You want?”
And more like, “Father, please don't interfere with what I want.”
And that is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle between us and God's will is not the devil.
Sometimes it is our unwillingness to surrender our own.
James understood this danger.
He wrote to believers who were confidently discussing their business plans, their travels, and the profits they expected to make.
They had destinations.
They had schedules.
They had financial expectations.
They had a future mapped out.
But something was missing from their calculations.
God.
James 4:13–15 records these words in the King James Version:
“Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.”
Notice what James did not condemn.
He did not condemn traveling.
He did not condemn business.
He did not condemn earning a profit.
He confronted the arrogance of planning as though tomorrow belonged to us.
In the Greek text, James uses the expression:
ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ — ean ho kyrios thelēsē
“If the Lord wills.”
Those words are not a magical phrase Christians must attach to every sentence to make their plans holy.
They describe a posture of the heart.
A recognition that God is Lord, that our lives depend upon Him, and that even our most carefully designed future remains subject to His wisdom.
James is not teaching believers to abandon planning.
He is teaching us to abandon the illusion of control.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because you can have a calendar filled with appointments and still have a heart surrendered to Christ.
You can pursue a career and still honor Jesus.
You can build a business, earn money, and provide generously for your family without making wealth your god.
The issue is not merely what you are building.
The issue is who sits on the throne of your heart while you build it.
There is a heartbreaking scene in Scripture that exposes this struggle.
A wealthy young man approached Jesus.
He was not presented as someone openly hostile to God.
He was serious about eternal life.
He knew the commandments.
He had a respectable moral history.
From the outside, he looked like the kind of person many religious communities would admire.
But Jesus saw something deeper.
Mark 10:21 says:

“Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.”
Do not miss those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before confronting the thing that held his heart captive, Jesus looked upon him with love.
This was not cruelty.
This was not an attempt to humiliate him.
This was the love of Christ exposing the one thing the man could not bear to surrender.

Jesus instructed this particular man to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him. The passage does not establish that every Christian must sell everything. It does reveal how deeply possessions can compete with devotion to God.
And the young man's response is devastating.
Mark 10:22 tells us:
“And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions.”
He came to Jesus wanting eternal life.
But when following Jesus threatened the treasure he could not release, he walked away grieving.
Think about that.
He stood before the One who could give him eternal life.
And he left because he could not surrender what he already possessed.
What if some of us are doing something similar?
Not necessarily with money.
Perhaps with a relationship we know is drawing us away from obedience.
Perhaps with an ambition that has consumed our identity.
Perhaps with an opportunity that promises recognition but requires dishonesty.
Perhaps with a business practice we keep justifying because it produces income.
Perhaps with a dream we have defended so fiercely that we no longer allow Scripture to challenge it.
We say, “God knows my heart.”
And He does.
That is precisely why we must examine it.
Because God sees not only our dreams, but also the motives we sometimes hide beneath them.
Proverbs 16:2 says:
“All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits.”
We are remarkably skilled at explaining our own behavior.
We can rename pride as confidence.
Greed as ambition.
Bitterness as discernment.
Disobedience as independence.
And selfishness as self-care.
Not every confident decision is prideful. Not every ambitious goal is greedy. But the human heart can disguise sinful motives beneath respectable language.
Sometimes we do not need another motivational message telling us to chase our dreams.
Sometimes we need the Word of God to ask why we are chasing them in the first place.
Why do you want that promotion?
Why do you want that platform?
Why do you want that relationship?
Why do you want people to notice your achievements?
Why does the thought of someone else succeeding make you uncomfortable?
Why does the possibility of losing your status frighten you more than the possibility of compromising your obedience?
These are not questions meant to crush you.
They are questions that may lead you toward freedom.
Because the Lord who exposes sin is also the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
And if something in your heart is becoming uncomfortable right now, do not rush to silence it.
Bring it honestly before Jesus.
There is another man in Scripture whose plans seemed perfectly reasonable.
He was wealthy.
His land produced abundantly.
He faced a problem many people would love to have: more crops than his existing storage could hold.
So he made a plan.
He would tear down his barns and build larger ones.
He would store his goods.
He would secure his future.
Then he would relax and enjoy what he had accumulated.
From a purely financial perspective, the plan might have appeared sensible.
But Jesus tells us something chilling.
In Luke 12:20, God says to the man:
“Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
The man had prepared for years of comfort.
But he had not reckoned with the uncertainty of his own life.
His tragedy was not that he owned a successful farm.
It was that he had made his abundance the center of his security while neglecting his responsibility before God.
Jesus concludes the parable in Luke 12:21:
“So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
That sentence should make every one of us examine what we call success.
Because you can have a full bank account and an impoverished spiritual life.
You can own a beautiful house and have a home starved of love.
You can build a respected reputation while hiding a pattern of sin.
You can be celebrated by strangers and neglect the people God has entrusted to your care.
You can gain the applause of a thousand people and lose the quiet joy of walking closely with Christ.
And one day, the achievements that consumed so much of your attention will no longer be able to answer the deepest questions of your soul.
Did I love God?
Did I love people?
Did I walk in truth?
Did I repent when I sinned?
Did I use what was entrusted to me faithfully?
Did I follow Jesus, or did I simply ask Him to accompany me wherever I wanted to go?
Jesus asked a question in Mark 8:36 that no amount of worldly success can silence:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
The world tells you to make a name for yourself.
Jesus calls you to follow Him.
The world tells you that your worth is measured by your achievements.
The Gospel tells you that sinners are reconciled to God through the saving work of Christ, not through impressive résumés.
The world tells you that you must never lose.
Jesus says in Mark 8:35 that whoever loses his life for His sake and the Gospel's will save it.
And this is where Christianity confronts something far deeper than poor planning.
It confronts the sinful human desire to be our own lord.
We want God's protection without always wanting His correction.
We want His promises without always embracing His commands.
We want His blessings while reserving the right to make the final decision.
But Jesus did not come merely to improve the plans of self-governing people.
He came to save sinners and make them His own.
And the cross reveals just how serious that salvation is.
Consider Jesus in Gethsemane.
The night before His crucifixion.
The betrayal approaching.
The suffering ahead.
The weight of what He was about to endure.
Jesus prayed in deep anguish.
Luke 22:42 records His words:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
In the Greek text, the central words are:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, not my will, but Yours be done.”
Here we must be careful not to reduce the holy agony of Gethsemane to an ordinary lesson about making career decisions.
Jesus was not merely demonstrating a useful planning strategy.
He was submitting to the Father's will as He approached the suffering through which He would accomplish redemption.
His obedience was unique in its saving purpose.
Yet His prayer also gives His followers a profound example of trust and surrender.
He did not treat the Father's will as an inconvenience.
He submitted to it.
And through His obedience unto death, the way of salvation was opened for sinners who could never save themselves.
Philippians 2:8 says that Christ:
“humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
This is the center of the Gospel.
Not that surrender makes all our dreams come true.
Not that obedience guarantees financial success.
Not that enough faith will make every obstacle disappear.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, so that everyone who repents and believes in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
That is greater than any promotion.
Greater than any business expansion.
Greater than any relationship status.
Greater than any earthly achievement.
And once you begin to understand what Jesus has done for you, another question rises in your heart.
If Christ gave Himself to save me, why am I treating surrendering my plans to Him as though He were trying to steal my happiness?
Perhaps you have been afraid to pray, “Lord, Your will be done.”
Because you know those words might change something.
They might change the way you pursue money.
They might change the way you treat your spouse.
They might change the kind of business opportunities you accept.
They might change your priorities, your habits, your relationships, or your understanding of success.
And change can be frightening.
Especially when you have spent years building a life around a particular dream.
Perhaps you are a parent working exhausting hours because you want your children to have opportunities you never had.
You are not wrong to want to provide for them.
But maybe somewhere along the way, providing things has begun replacing your presence.
Perhaps you are a young professional desperate to prove that you are not a failure.
You have endured rejection, criticism, and comparison.
You want to accomplish something meaningful.
But maybe your hunger for approval has grown louder than your desire to obey Christ.
Perhaps you are a business owner carrying the pressure of payroll, bills, debt, and responsibilities nobody else sees.
You pray for growth because people depend on you.
Yet perhaps there are decisions you need to examine—not because profit is evil, but because God calls you to pursue it without sacrificing integrity.
Or perhaps you are someone whose plans have already fallen apart.
You prayed.
You believed.
You waited.
And the door still closed.
The relationship ended.
The business failed.
The opportunity disappeared.
The future you imagined slipped through your hands.
And now you are wondering whether God has abandoned you.
Listen carefully.
A failed plan is not proof that God has rejected you. And a successful plan is not proof that God approves of everything you are doing.
Scripture does not allow us to interpret every circumstance so simply.
Faithful believers can suffer.
Disobedient people can prosper temporarily.
Open doors are not automatic endorsements from heaven.
Closed doors are not automatic judgments against you.
We need more than circumstances to discern what honors God.
We need His Word.
We need prayer.
We need humility.
We need wise counsel.
And we need hearts willing to obey even when obedience costs us something.
Proverbs 3:5–6 says:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.”
The Hebrew of Proverbs 3:6 contains the phrase:
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ
Bekhol-derakhekha da'ehu.
“In all your ways, acknowledge Him.”
The Hebrew verb translated “acknowledge” comes from יָדַע — yadaʿ, meaning “to know.”
In this context, it calls us to recognize God in every sphere of life, not merely to mention Him occasionally.
Not only at church.
Not only during worship.
Not only when disaster strikes.
In your work.
In your spending.
In your marriage.
In your conversations.
In your private decisions.
In your ambitions.
In your plans.
Every part of life belongs under His lordship.
And the promise that God will direct or make straight our paths is not a guarantee that life will be easy or that every personal ambition will succeed.
It is an invitation to trust His wisdom rather than making our limited understanding the final authority.
That means you do not have to know every detail of tomorrow to obey God today.
Sometimes the next faithful step is already clear.
Tell the truth.
End the dishonest arrangement.
Apologize.
Forgive.
Refuse the temptation.
Care for your family.
Keep your commitment.
Stop manipulating the situation.
Seek counsel.
Make the decision that agrees with Scripture, even if it is less profitable or less impressive.

And sometimes, when no clear moral command settles the choice, faithful Christians can prayerfully weigh their options and make responsible decisions without pretending they have received a secret message from heaven.
Surrender does not require us to become passive.
It requires us to become faithful.
But there is still one more question that may reach deeper than all the others.
What if you have already made the wrong plans?
What if you ignored warnings?
What if pride led you into decisions you now regret?
What if your ambition hurt people?
What if you pursued recognition at the expense of your family?
What if you compromised your convictions?
What if you have been asking God to bless something you knew was wrong?
Is it too late?
Look at Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
He believed he would stand firm.
But when fear pressed against him, he denied even knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memories.
The sound of his own voice denying the One he loved.
Luke 22:61 tells us that after Peter's third denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
And Peter remembered.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
His confidence had collapsed.
His failure was undeniable.
But his story was not over.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of His mercy.
And the Savior who restored Peter is the same risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance today.
This does not mean sin has no consequences.
It does not mean every damaged relationship will automatically be repaired or every lost opportunity returned.
It means that failure does not have to be the final word over a life surrendered to Christ.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about becoming more successful.
It is about something far greater.
From the shame of sin to the mercy of the Savior.
From self-rule to surrender.
From empty religion to genuine repentance and faith.
From a life built around ourselves to a life transformed by Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus does not merely offer to decorate our plans with religious language.
He calls us to follow Him.
And sometimes following Him means continuing faithfully with the work already in our hands.
Sometimes it means changing how we pursue that work.
Sometimes it means walking away from what Scripture reveals to be sinful.
And sometimes it means accepting that the future we wanted is not the future we will receive.
But in every circumstance, Christ remains worthy of our trust.
Colossians 3:17 says:
“And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.”
Whatsoever.
That includes the ordinary things.
The meetings nobody sees.
The honest work nobody applauds.
The sacrifices made quietly for your children.
The temptation you resist when no one would know.
The apology you offer even though your pride wants to defend itself.
The generosity you practice without announcing it.
The decision to remain faithful when compromise seems easier.
These things matter to God.
You do not have to become famous to glorify Him.
You do not have to become wealthy to serve Him.
You do not have to build a massive platform to live a meaningful Christian life.
A faithful mother praying with her child can glorify God.
A father choosing integrity over dishonest gain can glorify God.
A struggling believer turning away from hidden sin can glorify God.
A young person refusing to exchange biblical convictions for popularity can glorify God.
An ordinary worker serving faithfully can glorify God.
And a person whose plans have collapsed can still glorify God through trust, obedience, and perseverance.
Because your value before God is not measured by how impressive your future appears to other people.
The Christian's hope rests in Jesus Christ.
Not in a flawless record of personal achievement.
Not in a perfectly executed five-year plan.
Not in the approval of an audience.
But in the crucified and risen Savior.
So perhaps tonight, before you ask God to bless another plan, you need to pray differently.
Not with polished religious language.
Not with words designed to impress anyone.
Just honestly.
“Father, I have spent so much time asking You to bless what I want that I have not always stopped to ask whether what I want honors You.
“Search my heart.
“Expose the pride I keep defending.
“Show me where fear has been making my decisions.
“Forgive me for treating success as though it could save me.
“Teach me to seek Your kingdom first.
“If my plans are good, help me pursue them faithfully.
“If my motives are sinful, lead me to repentance.
“If my path is wrong, give me courage to turn.
“And if obedience costs me something I desperately wanted, remind me that Jesus Christ is worth more than anything I could lose.
“Not my will, but Yours be done.
“In Jesus' name, amen.”
And perhaps that prayer is the beginning of a change you have been resisting for a long time.
Not necessarily a dramatic change that everyone will notice.
Maybe it begins with one honest conversation.
One act of repentance.
One decision to stop compromising.
One evening spent with your family instead of chasing another hour of applause.
One moment when you open your Bible before opening another door.
One quiet surrender.
Because spiritual transformation is not always loud.
Sometimes it begins when a person who has spent years saying, “Lord, bless my plans,” finally says, “Lord, teach me to honor You with my life.”
And if this message has exposed something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not need to reveal private details or pretend you have already figured everything out.
Maybe it is, “I need to surrender.”
Maybe it is a testimony about how God used a disappointment to draw you closer to Christ.
Your words might encourage another believer who thought they were the only one struggling with these questions.
And please, do not allow this message to disappear into another endless scroll.
Return to it before your next major decision.
Read the Scriptures for yourself.
Examine your motives again.
Not because following a page saves anyone.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
But because daily exposure to Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, honest conviction, and sound discipleship can help us keep turning our attention toward Him.
And if Gospel Warrior has become part of your walk with Christ, I want to share something close to the heart of this ministry.
Every article, every devotional, every Scripture-centered message, and every discipleship resource requires time, care, and ongoing support.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
But believers who have the desire and financial ability to support faithful Christian ministry can glorify God through willing, generous giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
Not because a monthly payment guarantees a blessing.
But because you believe that helping make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to others is a meaningful way to serve Christ.
It is simply another opportunity to support the spread of biblical truth.
These products are not the heart of our mission.
Jesus Christ is.
The mission is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in faith, and walk more faithfully with the Lord.
Help a friend discover the free library.
And above all, keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because the goal is not merely to grow a page.
It is to help people grow in the knowledge of Christ.
One person reading Scripture again.
One weary believer finding encouragement to persevere.
One wandering heart turning toward repentance.
One family beginning to pray together.
One person discovering that forgiveness is found not in self-improvement, but in the Savior who died and rose again.
These are the things worth laboring for.
And now, as you reach the end of this article, return to the question that brought you here.
You want God to bless your plans.
But have you asked whether those plans honor Him?
Do not leave that question unanswered.
Take it into your prayer time.
Take it into your decisions.
Take it into the places where nobody sees what you choose.
And remember that the greatest blessing God has given His people is not the certainty that their earthly plans will succeed.
It is Jesus Christ Himself.
The One who forgives.
The One who redeems.
The One who calls us to repentance.
The One who transforms.
The One who is worthy of following even when the road ahead is uncertain.
Your plans may change.
Your circumstances may change.
Your understanding of success may change.
But the Lord Jesus Christ remains the same.
And one day, you may discover that the mercy you needed most was not God blessing everything you wanted—but Jesus teaching your heart to want Him above everything else.
